text: Serotonin syndrome comes from too much serotonin, so I'd stop anything suspected of adding more (serotonergic substances). No more MDMA or other stimulants, of course, but also no DXM cough syrup, the painkiller tramadol or the antibiotic linezolid. I'd hold off on even their prescribed antidepressant until a doctor says to restart it, whether it's an SSRI like Prozac or Zoloft, Effexor or another SNRI, or an MAOI. Ayahuasca and other harmala brews, like Syrian rue, act as MAOIs too. And don't forget the supplements people don't think of as drugs, like 5-HTP, St John's wort and SAM-e.
reader: the friend of someone who shows signs of serotonin syndrome (say MDMA on top of an antidepressant: twitching muscles, sweating, a racing heart), who has just read "So if you see any of these patterns, call medics." and now does these steps while help comes

marked.s: No more MDMA or other stimulants, of course, but also no DXM cough syrup, the painkiller tramadol or the antibiotic linezolid.
I'd hold off on even their prescribed antidepressant until a doctor says to restart it, whether it's an SSRI like Prozac, an SNRI like Effexor or an MAOI.
Ayahuasca and other harmala brews, like Syrian rue, act as MAOIs too, and don't forget the supplements people don't think of as drugs, like 5-HTP, St John's wort and SAM-e.
Poison control can help figure out which mix of drugs caused this, but they can't treat serotonin syndrome, so I'd call them once the ambulance is on its way.
This guide suggests niacin for ending a trip, and DMSO for brain injuries, seizures and chest pain, but I wouldn't use either one here.
Niacin is actually unsafe with serotonin syndrome.

marked.s: If the person is fully alert and able to swallow, I would give cyproheptadine early, since it blocks serotonin receptors.
I wouldn't wait to see whether it does before doing the other steps.

But if they feel a strong urge to keep moving (akathisia), I'd have them do some fidgeting (especially of the calf muscle, flexing the feet), which can soothe that urge without the over-activity risk.

Overstimulating also dehydrates them, but we can't give fluids unless they're fully alert, able to swallow and not vomiting, and then just small sips of an electrolyte drink (a hypertonic one, more concentrated than an ordinary one, may be required if they still have symptoms of lack of electrolytes).
